nodes.name: Software Reset
nodes.description: Register at offset 0x02F

fields.name: SWRESET_FOR_DAT
fields.raw: Software reset for DAT line. Only part of data circuit is reset. The following registers and bits are cleared by this bit: Buffer data port register: – Buffer is cleared and initialized. Present state register: – Buffer read enable – Buffer write enable – Read transfer active – Write transfer active – DAT line active – Command inhibit (DAT) Block gap control register: – Continue request – Stop at block gap request Normal interrupt status register: – Buffer read ready – Buffer write ready – Block gap event – Transfer complete 1 Reset 0 Work
fields.abstract: Software reset that clears the DAT line circuitry, resetting data transfer buffers, clearing buffer-related status bits in the present state register, block gap control settings, and buffer ready interrupt flags.

fields.name: SWRESET_FOR_CMD
fields.raw: Software reset for CMD line. Only part of command circuit is reset. The following registers and bits are cleared by this bit: Present state register: – Command inhibit (CMD) Normal interrupt status register: – Command complete 1 Reset 0 Work
fields.abstract: Software reset for the CMD line that clears command-related status bits including command inhibit and command complete indicators in the present state and normal interrupt status registers.

fields.name: SWRESET_FOR_ALL
fields.raw: Software reset for all. This reset affects the entire HC except for the card detection circuit. Register bits of type R, RW, RW1C, RWAC are cleared to 0. During its initialization, the HD set this bit to 1 to reset the HC. The HC reset this bit to 0 when Capabilities registers are valid and the HD can read them. Additional use of software reset for all may not affect the value of the Capabilities registers. If this bit is set to 1, the SDMMC card resets itself and must be re initialized by the HD. 1 Reset 0 Work
fields.abstract: Software reset control bit that resets the entire host controller except the card detection circuit, clearing R/RW/RW1C/RWAC register bits to 0, and is automatically cleared by hardware when Capabilities registers become valid.

nodes.name: Normal Interrupt Status
nodes.description: Register at offset 0x030

fields.name: REG_ERRORINTRSTS
fields.raw:
Error interrupt
If any of the bits in the Error interrupt status register are set, then this bit is set. Therefore the HD can test for an error by checking this bit first.
0: No error
1: Error
fields.abstract: Indicates whether any error condition exists by reflecting the combined status of all bits in the Error interrupt status register, allowing quick error detection through a single bit check.

fields.name: NORMALINTRSTS_BOOTCOMPLETE
fields.raw:
Boot terminate interrupt
This status is set if the boot operation get terminated.
0: Boot operation is not terminated.
1: Boot operation is terminated.
Note: SoC does not support Execute in Place from eMMC
fields.abstract: Boot terminate interrupt status indicating whether the boot operation has been terminated (1) or is still in progress (0).

fields.name: NORMALINTRSTS_RCVBOOTACK
fields.raw:
Boot ack rx
This status is set if the boot acknowledge is received from device.
0: Boot ack is not received.
1: Boot ack is received.
Note: SoC does not support Execute in Place from eMMC
fields.abstract: Indicates whether a boot acknowledge signal has been received from the eMMC device during boot operations.

fields.name: NORMALINTRSTS_RETUNINGEVENT
fields.raw:
Re-tuning event
This status is set if Re-tuning request in the Present state register changes from 0 to 1. Host controller requests host driver to perform re-tuning for next data transfer. Current data transfer (not large block count) can be completed without re-tuning.
1: Re-tuning is performed.
0: Re-tuning is not required.
Note: Re-tuning is not supported.
fields.abstract: Status flag indicating a re-tuning event occurred when the re-tuning request transitioned from 0 to 1, signaling the host controller requests re-tuning for the next data transfer (note: re-tuning is not supported in this implementation).

nodes.name: Error Interrupt Status
nodes.description: Register at offset 0x032

fields.name: ERRORINTRSTS_HOSTERROR
fields.raw: Target response error Occurs when detecting ERROR in m_hresp (DMA transaction). 0 No error 1 Error
fields.abstract: Indicates a target response error when an ERROR is detected on m_hresp during a DMA transaction.

fields.name: ERRORINTRSTS_ADMAERROR
fields.raw: DMA error This bit is set when the host controller detects errors during ADMA based data transfer. The state of the ADMA at an error occurrence is saved in the ADMA Error status register. 0 No error 1 Error
fields.abstract: Indicates when the host controller detects an error during ADMA-based data transfer, with the ADMA state at error occurrence saved in the ADMA Error Status register.

fields.name: ERRORINTRSTS_AUTOCMDERROR
fields.raw: Auto CMD error Auto CMD12 and Auto CMD23 use this error status. This bit is set when detecting that one of the bits D00-D04 in Auto CMD Error status register has changed from 0 to 1. In case of Auto CMD12, this bit is set to 1, not only when the errors in Auto CMD12 occur but also when Auto CMD12 is not executed due to the previous command error. 0 No error 1 Error
fields.abstract: Indicates an Auto CMD error occurred when any bit in the Auto CMD Error status register (D00-D04) transitions from 0 to 1, applicable to both Auto CMD12 and Auto CMD23 operations.

fields.name: ERRORINTRSTS_DATAENDBITERROR
fields.raw: Data end bit error Occurs when detecting 0 at the end bit position of read data which uses the DAT line or the end bit position of the CRC status. 0 No error 1 Error
fields.abstract: Indicates a data end bit error occurred when a 0 was detected at the end bit position of read data on the DAT line or at the end bit position of CRC status.

fields.name: ERRORINTRSTS_DATACRCERROR
fields.raw: Data CRC error Occurs when detecting CRC error when transferring read data which uses the DAT line or when detecting the write CRC status having a value of other than 010". 0 No error 1 Error"
fields.abstract: Indicates a CRC error detected during data transfer on the DAT line, either from read data or from write CRC status not equal to '010'.

fields.name: ERRORINTRSTS_DATATIMEOUTERROR
fields.raw: Data timeout error Occurs when detecting one of following timeout conditions: – Busy timeout for R1b, R5b type – Busy timeout after Write CRC status – Write CRC status timeout – Read data timeout 0 No error 1 Timeout
fields.abstract: Indicates a data timeout error occurred due to busy timeout for R1b/R5b responses, busy timeout after write CRC status, write CRC status timeout, or read data timeout conditions.

fields.name: ERRORINTRSTS_CMDINDEXERROR
fields.raw: Command index error Occurs if a command index error occurs in the command response. 0 No error 1 Error
fields.abstract: Indicates whether a command index error occurred in the command response, where 0 means no error and 1 indicates an error.

fields.name: ERRORINTRSTS_CMDENDBITERROR
fields.raw: Command end bit error Occurs when detecting that the end bit of a command response is 0. 0 No error 1 End bit error generated
fields.abstract: Indicates a command end bit error occurred when the end bit of a command response was detected as 0 instead of the expected value.

nodes.name: Normal Interrupt Status Enable
nodes.description: Register at offset 0x034

fields.name: NORMALINTRSTS_ENABLEREGBIT15
fields.raw:
Fixed to 0
The HC controls error interrupts using the Error interrupt status enable register.
fields.abstract: This bit is fixed to 0 as the host controller manages error interrupts through a separate Error Interrupt Status Enable register rather than this field.

fields.name: NORMALINTRSTS_ENABLEREGBIT14
fields.raw:
Boot terminate interrupt enable
0 Masked
1 Enabled
Note: SoC does not support Execute In Place from eMMC.
fields.abstract: Enables or masks the boot terminate interrupt signal in the normal interrupt status enable register.

fields.name: NORMALINTRSTS_ENABLEREGBIT13
fields.raw:
Boot ack rcv enable
0 Masked
1 Enabled
Note: SoC does not support Execute In Place from eMMC.
fields.abstract: Enables the boot acknowledge received interrupt status, where 0 masks the interrupt and 1 enables it.

fields.name: NORMALINTRSTS_ENABLEREGBIT12
fields.raw:
Re-tuning event status enable
0 Masked
1 Enabled
Note: Re-tuning is not supported.
fields.abstract: Re-tuning event status enable bit that controls whether re-tuning event status is masked or enabled, though re-tuning is not supported in this implementation.

fields.name: NORMALINTRSTS_ENABLEREGBIT11
fields.raw:
INT_C status enable
If this bit is set to 0, the host controller clears the interrupt request to the system. The host driver may clear this bit before servicing the INT_C and may set this bit again after all interrupt requests to INT_C pin are cleared to prevent inadvertent interrupts.
Note: INT_C is not supported.
fields.abstract: Enables the INT_C interrupt status reporting, allowing the host controller to generate or suppress interrupt requests to the system for the INT_C pin (not supported in this implementation).

fields.name: NORMALINTRSTS_ENABLEREGBIT10
fields.raw:
INT_B status enable
If this bit is set to 0, the host controller clears the interrupt request to the system. The host driver may clear this bit before servicing the INT_B and may set this bit again after all interrupt requests to INT_B pin are cleared to prevent inadvertent interrupts.
Note: INT_B is not supported.
fields.abstract: Enables the INT_B interrupt status reporting, allowing the host controller to generate or suppress INT_B interrupt requests to the system.

fields.name: NORMALINTRSTS_ENABLEREGBIT9
fields.raw:
INT_A status enable
If this bit is set to 0, the host controller clears the interrupt request to the system. The host driver may clear this bit before servicing the INT_A and may set this bit again after all interrupt requests to INT_A pin are cleared to prevent inadvertent interrupts.
Note: INT_A is not supported.
fields.abstract: Enables the INT_A interrupt status reporting, allowing the host controller to generate or suppress interrupt requests to the system for the INT_A pin (not supported in this implementation).

fields.name: SDHCREGSET_CARDINTSTSENA
fields.raw:
Card interrupt status enable
If this bit is set to 0, the HC clears interrupt request to the system. The card interrupt detection is stopped when this bit is cleared and restarted when this bit is set to 1. The HD may clear the card interrupt status enable before servicing the card interrupt and may set this bit again after all interrupt requests from the card are cleared to prevent inadvertent interrupts.
0 Masked
1 Enabled
fields.abstract: Enables or masks card interrupt status detection and system interrupt requests, where clearing stops detection and setting to 1 restarts it.

fields.name: SDHCREGSET_CARDREMSTSENA
fields.raw:
Card removal status enable
0 Masked
1 Enabled
fields.abstract: Enables the card removal status signal to indicate when a card has been removed from the SD host controller slot.

fields.raw: INT_A signal enable. 0 Masked. 1 Enabled. Note: INT_A is not supported.
fields.abstract: Enables or masks the INT_A signal interrupt status, though INT_A functionality is not supported.

fields.abstract: Card interrupt signal enable bit that controls whether card interrupt signals are masked (0) or enabled (1).

fields.name: AUTOCMDERRSTS_NEXTERROR
fields.raw:
Command not issued by Auto CMD12 error
Setting this bit to 1 means CMD_wo_DAT is not executed due to an Auto CMD12 error (D04- D01) in this register.
This bit is set to 0 when Auto CMD error is generated by Auto CMD23.
0 No error
1 Not issued
fields.abstract: Indicates that CMD_wo_DAT was not executed due to an Auto CMD12 error; set to 1 when command issuance fails due to Auto CMD12 errors, cleared when the error originates from Auto CMD23.

fields.name: AUTOCMDERRSTS_INDEXERROR
fields.raw:
Auto CMD index error
Occurs if the command index error occurs in response to a command.
0 No error
1 Error
fields.abstract: Indicates whether an auto command index error occurred in the response to a command, where 1 signifies an error was detected.

fields.name: AUTOCMDERRSTS_ENDBITERROR
fields.raw:
Auto CMD end bit error
Occurs when detecting that the end bit of command response is 0.
0 No error
1 End bit error generated
fields.abstract: Indicates whether an end bit error was detected in the auto command response, set when the expected end bit value of 1 is read as 0.

fields.name: AUTOCMDERRSTS_CRCERROR
fields.raw:
Auto CMD CRC error
Occurs when detecting a CRC error in the command response.
0 No error
1 CRC error generated
fields.abstract: Indicates whether a CRC error was detected in the response to an Auto CMD command, where 1 signifies a CRC error occurred.

nodes.name: Host Control 2
nodes.description: Register at offset 0x03E

fields.name: HOSTCTRL2_
fields.raw:
Preset value enable
As the operating sdmmccard_clk frequency and I/O driver strength depend on the host system implementation, it is difficult to determine these parameters in the standard host driver. When preset value enable is set to automatic. This bit enables the functions defined in the Preset value registers.
1 Automatic selection by preset value are enabled
0 sdmmccard_clk and driver strength are controlled by host driver
If this bit is set to 0, sdmmccard_clk frequency select and driver strength select in Host control 2 register are set by host driver.
If this bit is set to 1, sdmmccard_clk frequency Select and driver strength select in Host control 2 register are set by host controller as specified in the Preset value registers.
fields.abstract: Enables automatic selection of clock frequency and driver strength using preset value registers, or allows manual control by the host driver when disabled.

fields.name: HOSTCTRL2_
fields.raw:
Asynchronous interrupt enable
1 Enabled
0 Disabled
fields.abstract: Enables or disables asynchronous interrupt signaling for the host controller.

fields.name: HOSTCTRL2_
fields.raw:
Sampling clock select
1 Tuned clock is used to sample data
0 Fixed clock is used to sample data
Note: Tunning is not supported. This bit should always set to 0.
fields.abstract: Selects between tuned clock (1) or fixed clock (0) for data sampling, though tuning is not supported so this field should always be set to 0.

fields.name: HOSTCTRL2_
fields.raw:
Execute tuning
1 Execute tuning
0 Not tuned or tuning completed
Note: Tunning is not supported. This bit should always set to 0.
fields.abstract: Tuning execution control bit that should always be set to 0 as tuning is not supported in this implementation.

fields.name: HOSTCTRL2_
fields.raw:
Driver strength select
In 3.3V signaling, this field is not effective.
Note: This field is not effective as only 3.3V signaling is supported.
fields.abstract: Driver strength select field, which is not effective as only 3.3V signaling is supported.

fields.name: CORECFG_MAXBLKLENGTH
fields.raw: Max block length. This value indicates the maximum block size that the HD can read and write to the buffer in the HC. The buffer transfers this block size without wait cycles. Three sizes can be defined as indicated below. 00 512 bytes, 01 1024 bytes, 10 2048 bytes, 11 4096 bytes. Note: max 512 B block size is supported.
fields.abstract: Indicates the maximum block size (512B, 1KB, 2KB, or 4KB) that the host driver can read/write to the host controller buffer without wait cycles, with only 512-byte blocks supported.

fields.name: CORECFG_BASECLKFREQ
fields.raw: Base clock frequency of SDMMC_CLK. It's value is 8'b00110010 (50 MHz). 50 MHz is shown as reset value, but sdmmc_clk freq is 100 MHz. 50 MHz clk for SDMMC card and controller should be generated by software by dividing sdmmc_clk from 2. Note: Base clock frequency configuration is programmed in CORE_CONFIG.baseclkfreq_sdmmc_clk field.
fields.abstract: Base clock frequency for SDMMC_CLK, hardcoded to 50 MHz (0x32), though the actual sdmmc_clk runs at 100 MHz and software must divide by 2 to achieve the 50 MHz card interface clock.

fields.name: CORECFG_TIMEOUTCLKUNIT
fields.raw: Timeout clock unit. This bit shows the unit of base clock frequency used to detect data timeout error. 0 KHz, 1 MHz
fields.abstract: Indicates the unit of the timeout clock frequency used for data timeout error detection, where 0 represents KHz and 1 represents MHz.

fields.name: CORECFG_TIMEOUTCLKFREQ
fields.raw: Timeout clock frequency. This bit shows the base clock frequency used to detect data timeout error. It's value is 6'b000001. Because timeout clock unit is 1 MHz, so timeout clock frequency is 1 MHz.
fields.abstract: Indicates the base clock frequency for data timeout error detection, fixed at 1 MHz (value 0x01) with a timeout clock unit of 1 MHz.

fields.name: DMADEBUGBUS
fields.raw:
DMA_CTRL debug bus
hostintf_blocknextcmd - Command Complete indication from CMDCTRL module is set, the next command indication should be blocked
hostintf_abortcmdmode - When the Abort command is issued, the flag is set
hostintf_rdxferactive - This is set from the time the command Last Bit is issued or Block Gap Continue to the time the last block of data is sent to host
hostintf_enddataxfer - It is set when the end Data Transfer Complete Indications from the PIO/SDMA and ADMA2 state machines
hostintf_stopatblkgap - For write transfer, it is set from the PIO/SDMA and ADMA2 state machines. For read transfer, RegSet is used to generate Stop at BlkGap
hostwrdat_state - The WriteData state machine transfers the data to host interface
hostrddat_state - The ReadData state machine receives the data from host interface
hosttrans_state[1:0] - Host transfer state machine
adma2_state[3:0] - ADMA2 state machine
piosdma_state[2:0] - PIO/SDMA state machine
fields.abstract: DMA_CTRL debug bus providing status signals including command blocking state, abort mode flag, read transfer active indicator, and end data transfer completion indications from PIO/SDMA and ADMA2 state machines.

nodes.name: SD Host Controller 3.0 Compliance
nodes.description:
## SD Host Controller 3.0 Compliance (F_SD_HOST_3_0)

This feature indicates that the SDMMC Controller implements the SD Host Controller Standard Specification Version 3.0, ensuring compatibility with the standardized register interface, command protocols, and operational modes defined by the SD Association. The controller provides the complete SD Host Controller 3.0 register set including command/response handling, data transfer modes (PIO/DMA/SDMA), clock control, power management, and interrupt mechanisms as specified in the standard. As a P0 core compliance feature, this forms the foundational architecture upon which all other SDMMC functionality is built, guaranteeing interoperability with standard SD/SDIO/eMMC device drivers and software stacks.

nodes.name: MMC 4.51 Support
nodes.description:
## MMC 4.51 Support (F_MMC_4_51)

**Feature Description:**

This feature provides compliance with the JEDEC MMC (MultiMediaCard) specification version 4.51, enabling the SDMMC Controller to interface with eMMC (embedded MMC) devices commonly used for non-volatile storage in automotive and industrial applications. The controller implements the required command set, timing modes, and protocol extensions defined in MMC 4.51, including support for high-speed modes (HS200/HS400 where applicable), boot operations, and enhanced device management features. As a P0 core compliance feature, this ensures the host controller can properly enumerate, configure, and communicate with MMC 4.51-compliant memory devices through the appropriate register configurations in HOSTCONTROL1, CLOCKCONTROL, and TRANSFERMODE registers.

nodes.name: 3MCR Multi Card Reader
nodes.description:
## 3MCR Multi Card Reader (F_3MCR)

The 3MCR (Multi Card Reader) is the core SDMMC host controller module that provides a complete interface for communicating with SD, SDIO, and MMC memory cards. It implements the SD Host Controller Standard Specification, featuring a comprehensive register set for command/response handling, data transfer control via PIO or DMA modes, configurable clock generation, and timeout management.

The controller architecture includes dedicated blocks for command control, transmit/receive data paths, a block buffer (FIFO) for data staging, and supports both single and multi-block transfers with programmable block sizes and automatic CRC generation/checking.

nodes.name: Command Issuing
nodes.description:
## Command Issuing (F_CMD_ENGINE)

The Command Issuing feature implements the core command control logic that manages the transmission of SD/MMC commands to connected cards through the CMD line interface. This engine handles command serialization, CRC generation, response reception and parsing, and coordinates with the timeout control block to detect command completion or timeout conditions. It interfaces with the COMMAND register (section 57.3.2.7) and ARGUMENT1 register (section 57.3.2.5) to construct and issue commands, storing received responses in the RESPONSEn registers (section 57.3.2.8) while signaling completion status through the interrupt system.

nodes.name: Auto CMD12
nodes.description:
## F_AUTO_CMD12: Auto CMD12 Feature

### Purpose
The Auto CMD12 feature enables the SDMMC host controller to automatically issue a CMD12 (STOP_TRANSMISSION) command at the end of a multiple-block data transfer without software intervention. This is a critical command engine optimization that reduces CPU overhead and ensures proper termination of multi-block read/write operations.

### Technical Behavior
When enabled via the Transfer Mode register (TRANSFERMODE), the controller automatically generates and transmits CMD12 after the specified block count has been transferred, properly terminating the multi-block operation. The command control logic (section 57.2.2.7) handles the CMD12 timing and response processing internally, with completion status reported through the normal interrupt status mechanism to indicate whether the auto-issued stop command completed successfully or encountered an error.

nodes.name: Auto CMD23
nodes.description:
## F_AUTO_CMD23 (Auto CMD23)

### Purpose
The Auto CMD23 feature enables the SDMMC host controller to automatically issue a CMD23 (SET_BLOCK_COUNT) command prior to executing a multi-block read or write operation, without requiring separate software intervention for each command sequence.

### Behavior
When enabled via the Transfer Mode register (TRANSFERMODE), the controller automatically prepends CMD23 to multi-block data transfer commands (CMD18 for read, CMD25 for write), using the value in the Argument 2 register (SDMASYSADDR) as the block count parameter. This hardware-automated command sequencing reduces software overhead, improves transfer efficiency, and ensures proper block count pre-definition as required by SD/eMMC specifications for reliable multi-block operations. The feature is particularly important for ADMA2 transfers where predefined block counts enable more deterministic DMA behavior and eliminate the need for open-ended transfers terminated by CMD12.

nodes.name: Data Transfer
nodes.description:
## F_DATA_TRANSFER: Data Transfer

**Description:**
The Data Transfer feature encompasses the core data movement capabilities of the SDMMC Controller, enabling read and write operations between the host system and SD/MMC cards. This includes support for both PIO (Programmed I/O) and DMA transfer modes, utilizing the block buffer for data staging, and managing single-block and multi-block transfers through the Transmit Control and Receive Control blocks. The feature handles data flow through the DATAPORT register, manages block size/count configuration via BLOCKSIZE and BLOCKCOUNT registers, and coordinates with the TRANSFERMODE register to configure transfer direction, auto-command execution, and DMA enable settings.

nodes.name: Non-DMA Transfer (PIO)
nodes.description:
## Non-DMA Transfer (PIO) (F_NON_DMA)

**Purpose:** Non-DMA Transfer (PIO) enables Programmed I/O data transfers where the CPU directly reads from or writes to the SDMMC controller's Data Port register (DATAPORT) to move data between system memory and the SD/MMC card, without using DMA hardware assistance.

**Behavior:** In PIO mode, the host controller generates Buffer Read Ready or Buffer Write Ready interrupts when the internal block buffer requires servicing, and the CPU must respond by performing sequential accesses to the DATAPORT register to transfer data. Section 57.2.2.3 describes the PIO/DMA controller that manages this process, while section 57.2.6 details the FIFO overrun and underrun conditions that can occur if the CPU cannot service the buffer quickly enough during non-DMA transfers.

nodes.name: SDMA Transfer
nodes.description:
## F_SDMA: SDMA Transfer

**Purpose:** SDMA (Single-operation DMA) Transfer enables automated data movement between system memory and the SDMMC controller's block buffer without continuous CPU intervention, using a simple linear addressing scheme for single-block or multi-block transfers.

**Behavior:** The SDMA system operates through the SDMASYSADDR register (57.3.2.2), which holds the system memory address for DMA transfers. When a data transfer is initiated with DMA enabled in the Transfer Mode register, the controller automatically reads from or writes to the specified memory address, generating a DMA interrupt at block boundaries to allow the host driver to update the system address for the next data segment. This mechanism, described in the PIO/DMA controller block (57.2.2.3), handles FIFO management and prevents overrun/underrun conditions (57.2.6) by coordinating data flow between the external memory bus and the internal block buffer.

nodes.name: ADMA1 Transfer
nodes.description:
## ADMA1 Transfer (F_ADMA1)

Based on the SPC58 H-Line SDMMC Controller specification, ADMA1 (Advanced DMA version 1) Transfer is a DMA mode that provides enhanced data transfer capabilities compared to basic SDMA by supporting descriptor-based scatter-gather operations with a simplified 32-bit descriptor format. ADMA1 allows the host controller to automatically process a linked list of descriptors, enabling transfers to/from non-contiguous memory regions without CPU intervention, though with the limitation of 4KB page-aligned boundaries. This mode is configured through the DMA Select field in the Host Control 1 register (HOSTCONTROL1) and operates in conjunction with the ADMA System Address register to manage descriptor fetching and data movement.

nodes.name: ADMA2 Transfer
nodes.description:
Based on the SPC58 H-Line Reference Manual for the SDMMC Controller (3MCR), here is the description for the ADMA2 Transfer feature:

## F_ADMA2: ADMA2 Transfer

**Description:** ADMA2 (Advanced DMA version 2) Transfer provides an enhanced DMA mechanism that uses descriptor tables in system memory to define scatter-gather data transfers, allowing non-contiguous memory buffers to be transferred efficiently without CPU intervention. The DMA mode is selected via the HOSTCONTROL1 register's DMA Select field, and ADMA2 operations utilize the descriptor-based architecture managed through the PIO/DMA controller block to handle complex multi-block data transfers with automatic address management. This P0-priority feature is essential for high-performance data transfer operations, eliminating the FIFO overrun/underrun conditions that can occur in non-DMA modes by providing autonomous data movement between the block buffer and system memory.

nodes.name: Multiple Block Transfer
nodes.description:
## Multiple Block Transfer (F_MULTI_BLOCK)

**Purpose:** This feature enables the SDMMC controller to transfer multiple consecutive data blocks in a single operation, significantly improving throughput for large data transfers to/from SD/MMC cards.

**Behavior:** Multiple block transfers are configured through the BLOCKCOUNT register (which specifies the number of blocks to transfer) and the TRANSFERMODE register (which enables multi-block mode and optional block count functionality). The controller automatically manages sequential block addressing and can utilize the Block Gap Control register (BLOCKGAPCONTROL) to pause transfers between blocks if needed, while the hardware handles block counting and transfer completion detection without continuous software intervention.

nodes.name: Single Block Transfer
nodes.description:
## Single Block Transfer (F_SINGLE_BLOCK)

Single Block Transfer enables the SDMMC controller to read or write exactly one data block (typically 512 bytes for SD cards) in a single command operation. This mode is configured via the Transfer Mode register (TRANSFERMODE) with the Multi/Single Block Select bit cleared, and the Block Count register (BLOCKCOUNT) set to 1, using commands like CMD17 (READ_SINGLE_BLOCK) or CMD24 (WRITE_BLOCK). This transfer type is fundamental for simple data operations where only one block needs to be accessed, avoiding the overhead of multi-block setup and the requirement for explicit stop commands (CMD12).

nodes.name: Abort Transaction
nodes.description:
## Abort Transaction (F_ABORT)

### Purpose
The Abort Transaction feature provides a mechanism to forcibly terminate an ongoing data transfer operation on the SDMMC controller, allowing the host to recover from error conditions, timeouts, or to cancel transfers that are no longer needed.

### Technical Behavior
This feature is typically implemented through the **Software Reset Register (SOFTWARERESET)** which contains bits to reset specific portions of the controller—specifically the command line (RSTCMD) and data line (RSTDAT) reset functions. When a data transfer must be aborted, the host issues an abort command (CMD12 for multi-block transfers) and may need to perform a software reset of the data circuit to clear the data path and restore the controller to a known state. The abort mechanism works in conjunction with the **Block Gap Control Register (BLOCKGAPCONTROL)** which can stop transfers at block boundaries, and the **Present State Register (PRESENTSTATE)** which indicates when command and data lines are available after the abort completes.

nodes.name: Suspend/Resume
nodes.description:
## Suspend/Resume (F_SUSPEND_RESUME)

The Suspend/Resume feature enables the host controller to temporarily halt an ongoing multi-block data transfer at a block gap boundary and later resume it, allowing the host to service higher-priority operations or manage bus arbitration in multi-card scenarios. This functionality is controlled through the **Block Gap Control register (BLOCKGAPCONTROL)**, which provides bits to request a stop at the next block gap and to subsequently continue the suspended transfer.

When a suspend is requested, the controller completes the current block transfer, pauses at the gap, and signals the host via interrupt; the host can then issue CMD52 (for SDIO) or CMD12 to formally suspend the card before resuming with the appropriate continue command or register write.

nodes.name: Interrupt System
nodes.description:
## Interrupt System (F_INTERRUPT)

The SDMMC Controller implements a comprehensive interrupt system that signals the host processor about various controller events including command completion, data transfer completion, buffer ready states, card insertion/removal, and error conditions. The interrupt architecture uses status registers (Normal Interrupt Status and Error Interrupt Status) combined with corresponding enable registers to allow selective masking of individual interrupt sources. This system enables efficient event-driven operation for both PIO and DMA transfer modes, eliminating the need for continuous polling while providing immediate notification of transfer completion, timeouts, CRC errors, and other critical events requiring software attention.

nodes.name: Normal Interrupts
nodes.description:
## Normal Interrupts (F_NORMAL_INT)

Normal Interrupts in the SDMMC Controller represent the standard operational interrupt sources that signal successful completion of expected events during SD/MMC card transactions. These interrupts are managed through the Normal Interrupt Status register (NORMALINTSTATUS) and include events such as command complete, transfer complete, buffer read/write ready, card insertion/removal, and DMA interrupt conditions.

The host software enables specific normal interrupts via the Normal Interrupt Status Enable and Normal Interrupt Signal Enable registers, allowing selective notification of completed operations without polling. When enabled and triggered, these interrupts facilitate efficient programmed I/O and DMA-based data transfers by signaling the CPU only when attention is required for the next phase of a transaction.

nodes.name: Error Interrupts
nodes.description:
## Error Interrupts (F_ERROR_INT)

Based on the SDMMC Controller (3MCR) specification for the SPC58 H-Line, Error Interrupts provide notification mechanisms for various fault conditions that can occur during SD/MMC card operations. These interrupts signal error events such as command timeout, command CRC errors, command end bit errors, command index errors, data timeout, data CRC errors, data end bit errors, and FIFO overrun/underrun conditions as described in section 57.2.6.

The Error Interrupt functionality is managed through dedicated interrupt status and enable registers (referenced in section 57.3.2.17-57.3.2.18), allowing software to detect, mask, and respond to specific error conditions during command execution and data transfers. As a P0 priority feature under the parent interrupt system (F_INTERRUPT), these error notifications are critical for implementing robust error handling and recovery mechanisms in the host driver software.

nodes.name: Wakeup Event
nodes.description:
## Wakeup Event (F_WAKEUP)

The Wakeup Event feature enables the SDMMC controller to generate interrupt signals that can wake the system from low-power states when specific card-related events occur. This functionality is configured through the Wake Up Control Register (WAKEUPCONTROL), which allows enabling wakeup on card insertion, card removal, or card interrupt conditions.

When enabled, these wakeup events trigger the normal interrupt status mechanism (as a child of F_INTERRUPT) while simultaneously asserting a wakeup signal to the system power management logic, allowing the host to resume operation and service the SD/MMC card without requiring the system to remain in an active power state during idle periods.

nodes.name: Clock Control
nodes.description:
## Clock Control (F_CLOCK_CONTROL)

The Clock Control feature manages the SD clock generation and distribution to connected SD/MMC cards through the CLOCKCONTROL register, enabling software to start/stop the clock signal, select clock frequencies via divider settings, and monitor clock stability. This feature interfaces with the internal clock generator block (section 57.2.2.5) to provide programmable clock frequencies within the supported frequency range (section 57.2.5), which is essential for proper card initialization sequences and data transfer operations. As a P0 priority feature, it provides fundamental clock domain control including internal clock enable, SD clock output enable, and clock divider configuration for meeting various SD/MMC timing specifications.

nodes.name: SDCLK Frequency Select
nodes.description:
## SDCLK Frequency Select (F_SDCLK_FREQ_SEL)

**Purpose:** This feature controls the frequency divider settings for the SD Card Clock (SDCLK) output signal, allowing software to configure the appropriate clock speed for SD/MMC card communication during initialization and data transfer phases.

**Behavior:** The SDCLK Frequency Select field within the Clock Control Register (CLOCKCONTROL) specifies a divisor value applied to the base clock to generate the SDCLK frequency. During card initialization, a lower frequency (typically 400 kHz or less) must be selected, while higher frequencies (up to the card's maximum supported rate) can be configured after successful initialization. The clock generator block (section 57.2.2.5) uses this programmed divisor to produce the appropriate SDCLK output within the supported frequency range defined in section 57.2.5.

nodes.name: Power Control
nodes.description:
## F_POWER_CONTROL (Power Control)

The Power Control feature manages the SD card bus power supply through the **Power Control Register (POWERCONTROL)**, enabling the host controller to turn the SD card power on or off and select the appropriate voltage level for the connected card. This is a fundamental P0 priority feature required for proper card initialization, as the SD/MMC specification mandates specific power sequencing during card detection and enumeration. The controller uses this register to control the external power supply circuitry, supporting voltage switching between different levels (typically 3.3V and 1.8V) as required by the card type and operating mode.

nodes.name: Speed Mode Support
nodes.description:
## Speed Mode Support (F_SPEED_MODES)

This feature provides support for multiple SD/MMC bus speed modes, enabling the SDMMC controller to operate at different clock frequencies and data transfer rates as defined by SD/MMC specifications. The controller supports Default Speed (DS), High Speed (HS), and potentially UHS-I speed modes, with the Clock Control register (CLOCKCONTROL) managing clock frequency selection and the Host Control 1 register (HOSTCONTROL1) configuring the high-speed enable bit for mode switching. Speed mode configuration directly impacts the maximum achievable data throughput and must be coordinated with proper voltage signaling levels and card capability negotiation.

nodes.name: Default Speed (25 MHz)
nodes.description:
## F_DEFAULT_SPEED: Default Speed (25 MHz)

**Purpose:** This feature implements the baseline SD card operating mode where the SDMMC controller operates the SD bus clock at up to 25 MHz, providing standard data transfer rates as defined by the SD specification for backward compatibility with all SD/MMC cards.

**Behavior:** The Default Speed mode is configured through the Clock Control Register (CLOCKCONTROL) by setting the appropriate SDCLK Frequency Select bits to achieve a 25 MHz clock output. This mode uses single data rate (SDR) signaling on the 4-bit data bus, yielding a maximum theoretical throughput of 12.5 MB/s, and serves as the mandatory fallback mode that all compliant cards must support during initialization and normal operation.

nodes.name: High Speed (50 MHz)
nodes.description:
## High Speed (50 MHz) - F_HIGH_SPEED

### Description
The High Speed mode enables the SDMMC Controller to operate at clock frequencies up to 50 MHz, providing enhanced data transfer rates compared to the default speed mode (25 MHz). This mode is configured through the Host Control 1 register (HOSTCONTROL1) by setting the High Speed Enable bit, and requires proper clock divider configuration in the Clock Control register (CLOCKCONTROL) to achieve the target 50 MHz frequency within the controller's supported frequency range.

### Technical Details
When High Speed mode is enabled, the controller doubles the maximum clock frequency from the default 25 MHz to 50 MHz, effectively doubling the theoretical data throughput for SD card communications. The clock generator block must be properly configured to derive the 50 MHz clock from the base clock source while maintaining signal integrity requirements for high-speed SD card interface timing.

nodes.name: UHS-I SDR12
nodes.description:
## UHS-I SDR12 (F_UHS_SDR12)

**Feature Description:**

UHS-I SDR12 is the baseline Ultra High Speed mode for SD cards operating at 1.8V signaling, providing Single Data Rate transfers at a maximum clock frequency of 25 MHz with a theoretical throughput of up to 12.5 MB/s. This mode serves as the mandatory fallback UHS-I speed mode that all UHS-I compliant cards and hosts must support, ensuring basic interoperability when higher speed modes cannot be negotiated.

The SDR12 mode is configured through the Host Control 2 register's UHS Mode Select field and requires successful completion of the 1.8V signaling voltage switch sequence before operation, as specified in the SD Physical Layer Specification for UHS-I interface timing requirements.

nodes.name: UHS-I SDR25
nodes.description:
## UHS-I SDR25 (F_UHS_SDR25)

**Feature Description:**

UHS-I SDR25 is a Ultra High Speed mode that operates using Single Data Rate signaling at 50 MHz clock frequency, achieving a maximum bus speed of 50 MB/s on a 4-bit data bus. This mode requires 1.8V signaling voltage (enabled through the Host Control 2 register's 1.8V Signaling Enable bit) and represents the baseline UHS-I speed grade that doubles the throughput of legacy High Speed mode while maintaining single-edge data sampling.

The SDR25 mode is configured through the UHS Mode Select field in the Host Control 2 register and requires successful completion of the voltage switching sequence from 3.3V to 1.8V signaling before operation.

nodes.name: UHS-I SDR50
nodes.description:
## UHS-I SDR50 (F_UHS_SDR50)

**Feature Description:**

UHS-I SDR50 is a Ultra High Speed mode that operates using Single Data Rate signaling at 100 MHz clock frequency, achieving a maximum data transfer rate of 50 MB/s on the SD bus. This mode requires 1.8V signaling voltage (enabled through the voltage switching sequence) and utilizes the standard 4-bit data bus width with data sampled on the rising edge of the clock only.

SDR50 mode is configured through the Host Control 2 register's UHS Mode Select field and requires the controller to support the 1.8V signaling capability indicated in the Capabilities register. The mode may optionally use tuning to optimize sampling point timing, depending on the controller implementation and signal integrity requirements at the 100 MHz operating frequency.

nodes.name: UHS-I SDR104
nodes.description:
## UHS-I SDR104 (F_UHS_SDR104)

**Feature Description:**

UHS-I SDR104 is the highest performance Ultra High Speed mode supported by the SDMMC controller, enabling single data rate transfers at up to 208 MB/s using a 208 MHz clock frequency on the SD interface. This mode requires 1.8V signaling voltage (achieved through the voltage switching procedure) and utilizes the 4-bit data bus width with tuning to compensate for signal timing variations at these high frequencies.

SDR104 mode is configured through the UHS Mode Select field in the Host Control 2 register, and the controller must successfully complete the tuning procedure (using CMD19) to calibrate the sampling point before data transfers can reliably operate at this speed. The Capabilities register indicates whether the host controller supports SDR104 mode, and proper clock divider settings in the Clock Control register are required to achieve the target 208 MHz operation.

nodes.name: UHS-I DDR50
nodes.description:
## UHS-I DDR50 (F_UHS_DDR50)

**Description:**
UHS-I DDR50 is an Ultra High Speed mode that enables double data rate (DDR) signaling at 50 MHz clock frequency, achieving an effective data transfer rate of up to 50 MB/s by sampling data on both rising and falling clock edges. This mode operates at 1.8V signaling voltage and requires the host controller to configure the UHS Mode Select field in the Host Control 2 register to enable DDR operation with the appropriate timing parameters. DDR50 provides improved throughput compared to SDR modes while maintaining compatibility with UHS-I SD cards that support this speed class.

nodes.name: Boot Operation
nodes.description:
## Boot Operation (F_BOOT_OP)

Based on the SDMMC Controller (3MCR) specification for the SPC58 H-Line, the Boot Operation feature enables the host controller to support MMC boot mode, allowing the system to boot directly from an eMMC/MMC device. This functionality permits the controller to read boot data from the MMC card's boot partition during system initialization, typically using a pre-boot or alternative boot sequence defined by the MMC specification. The feature is essential for embedded systems requiring fast, reliable boot-from-flash capability without requiring a separate boot ROM or external memory interface.

nodes.name: Alternative Boot Mode
nodes.description:
## Alternative Boot Mode (F_ALT_BOOT)

**Purpose:** Alternative Boot Mode provides a secondary boot mechanism for eMMC devices that differs from the mandatory boot mode, allowing the host controller to initiate boot operations using a different command sequence where CMD0 with argument 0xFFFFFFFA is used instead of holding CMD low.

**Behavior:** In Alternative Boot Mode, the SDMMC controller initiates the boot sequence by sending a specific boot command rather than using the continuous CMD line assertion method. This mode is configured through the HOSTCONTROL2 register's boot-related fields and the MMCBOOT register, enabling the controller to read boot data from the eMMC device's boot partition using standard command/response protocols while still supporting boot acknowledgment detection and boot data transfer completion signaling.

**Context:** As a child feature of F_BOOT_OP, this provides an alternative approach to eMMC boot operations that may be preferred in certain system configurations or when the mandatory boot mode's CMD line timing requirements cannot be met.

nodes.name: Software Reset
nodes.description:
## F_SOFTWARE_RESET (Software Reset)

**Purpose:** The Software Reset feature provides software-controlled reset capability for the SDMMC Controller, allowing the host driver to reset specific functional blocks or the entire controller without requiring a hardware reset.

**Behavior:** This feature is implemented through the Software Reset Register (SOFTWARERESET) as described in section 57.3.2.17, enabling selective reset of controller components such as the command line, data line, or a complete controller reset. When triggered, the reset operation clears pending operations, resets internal state machines, and returns the affected blocks to their initial state, which is essential for error recovery scenarios or reinitializing the controller during runtime without affecting the entire system.

nodes.name: Timeout Control
nodes.description:
## Timeout Control (F_TIMEOUT_CONTROL)

The Timeout Control feature manages the data timeout counter in the SDMMC host controller, which monitors the interval between data transfers on the DAT line to detect communication failures with SD/MMC cards. It uses a configurable timeout value (set via the TIMEOUTCONTROL register) that determines the maximum allowable time for data line activity, generating a Data Timeout Error interrupt if the card fails to respond within the specified period. This mechanism is essential for robust error handling, preventing the host controller from waiting indefinitely when cards become unresponsive or are removed during data operations.

nodes.name: Capabilities Register
nodes.description:
## Capabilities Register (F_CAPABILITIES)

The Capabilities Register is a read-only control register that reports the hardware capabilities and supported features of the SDMMC host controller, including supported voltage levels, maximum block length, base clock frequency, timeout clock frequency, and DMA support capabilities. This register allows software to query the controller's fixed hardware configuration at runtime to properly initialize and configure the host controller for communication with SD/MMC cards. As a P0 priority control feature, it is essential for system initialization since drivers must read these capabilities before configuring operational parameters like clock speeds, power settings, and transfer modes.

nodes.name: Preset Value Registers
nodes.description:
## Preset Value Registers (F_PRESET_VALUES)

The Preset Value Registers provide pre-configured settings for different SD/MMC speed modes, allowing the host controller to automatically apply optimal clock divider, driver strength, and other timing parameters when switching between speed modes (such as Default Speed, High Speed, SDR12, SDR25, SDR50, SDR104, and DDR50). These registers eliminate the need for software to manually calculate and configure timing parameters for each speed mode, enabling faster and more reliable mode transitions.

When the Preset Value Enable bit is set in the Host Control 2 register, the controller automatically loads the appropriate preset values based on the selected UHS mode, streamlining speed mode configuration and ensuring compliance with SD specification timing requirements.

nodes.name: 1.8V Signaling
nodes.description:
## 1.8V Signaling (F_VOLTAGE_SWITCH)

This feature enables the SDMMC controller to switch from the default 3.3V signaling voltage to 1.8V signaling, which is mandatory for Ultra High Speed (UHS) modes such as SDR50, SDR104, and DDR50. The voltage switching sequence is controlled through the Power Control register (POWERCONTROL), which manages the SD Bus Voltage Select field and coordinates the signaling voltage transition with the connected SD card. This capability is essential for achieving higher data transfer rates while reducing power consumption, as UHS-I cards require 1.8V signaling to operate in their enhanced speed modes.

nodes.name: 4-bit Data Bus
nodes.description:
## 4-bit Data Bus (F_4BIT_MODE)

This feature enables the SDMMC controller to transfer data using a 4-bit wide data bus (DAT[3:0]) instead of the default 1-bit mode, providing up to 4x improvement in data throughput. The data bus width is configured through the **Host Control 1 register (HOSTCONTROL1)** by setting the Data Transfer Width bit, which switches the controller between 1-bit and 4-bit data transfer modes. This capability is essential for achieving higher performance with SD cards that support wider bus widths, as specified in the SD Memory Card specification.

nodes.name: 8-bit Data Bus (MMC)
nodes.description:
## 8-bit Data Bus (MMC) (F_8BIT_MODE)

**Purpose:** This feature enables the SDMMC controller to operate with an 8-bit wide data bus when interfacing with MMC (MultiMediaCard) devices, doubling the data transfer bandwidth compared to the standard 4-bit mode.

**Behavior:** The 8-bit data bus mode is configured through the Host Control 1 register (HOSTCONTROL1), specifically using the Extended Data Transfer Width bit. When enabled, the controller utilizes all 8 data lines (DAT[7:0]) for parallel data transfers, which is a capability specific to MMC/eMMC devices as SD cards are limited to 4-bit maximum bus width. This mode is essential for achieving high-speed data throughput in embedded MMC applications, particularly when operating in HS200 or HS400 modes.

nodes.name: LED Control
nodes.description:
## LED Control (F_LED_CONTROL)

Based on the SDMMC Controller specification, the LED Control feature provides a mechanism to indicate SD/MMC card activity through an external LED signal. This functionality is typically controlled via a bit in the **Host Control 1 register (HOSTCONTROL1)**, which allows software to enable or disable the LED output that reflects bus activity such as data transfers or command operations.

The LED control signal is part of the bus interface group and serves as a visual indicator for system designers to monitor card access status, commonly used during debugging or to provide user feedback about storage device activity on the SD/MMC bus.

Introduction
RM0452
58/3897
RM0452 Rev 4
2 
Introduction
2.1 
SPC58xHx microcontroller
The SPC58xHx MCU is the top featured microcontroller in a new family of devices 
superseding the SPC5x family. SPC58xHx builds on the legacy of the SPC5x family, while 
introducing new features coupled with higher throughput to provide substantial reduction of 
cost per feature and significant power and performance improvement (MIPS per mW). On 
the SPC58xHx microcontroller there are up to three e200z425 processor cores, one 
checker and one e200z0 core embedded in the Hardware Security Module.
         
2.1.1 
Overall architecture
The architecture is split into two computing shells as shown in Table 2. The processing shell 
consists of one pair of CPU in lock-step for safety, one CPU without lock-step, a DMA move 
engine, fast local memories inside the CPUs and fast system memory, a Hardware Security 
Module (HSM) and all peripherals connected through a crossbar switch (XBAR_1).
The streaming shell consists of one CPU (no lock-step), a DMA move engine, fast local 
memories inside the CPU, fast system memories, and all the other peripherals connected 
through a crossbar switch (XBAR_0).
2.1.2 
Core features
The processing shell consists of dual e200z4256n3 CPUs operating up to 200 MHz, one 
core being paired with a safety checker core in delayed lock-step mode.
The streaming shell includes a e200z4256n3 CPU operating upto 200 MHz.
All cores from processing shell and streaming shell have the same feature set including 
enhancements to implement Digital Signal Processing (DSP) algorithms, called “LSP” 
(Lightway Signal Processing block).
The fifth programmable CPU is a e200z0 running up to 100 MHz and is embedded in the 
HSM.

All CPUs are compatible with the Power Architecture VLE instruction set, that supports code 
size reduction. The Power Architecture has enhancements that improve the architecture’s fit 
in embedded applications.
Note:
The e200z0 core is embedded in the Hardware Security Module.
2.1.3 
Core_2
The Core_2 is one of five processor cores on the SPC58xHx device as shown in Table 2. In 
general, the intended use of the Core_2 is to initially configure the machine and then control 
various peripheral elements of the device. However, the Core_2 is not limited to any 
particular duty.
The data and the instruction bus structures of the Core_2, which consist of a 64-bit data bus 
and a 32-bit address bus, are connected to a Crossbar Switch XBAR_1 which operates at 
200 MHz.
The Core_2 is automatically started during the boot-up sequence after the release of 
RESET. This process is fully described in Chapter 8: Reset and Boot.
The Core_2 is placed in the SPC58xHx architecture in such a way that enables it to access 
many of the peripheral elements without affecting the processing speed of Core_0 and 
Core_1. On the SPC58xHx device there are several A/D channels taking data which must 
be analyzed for various spectral components.
This specificity associated with its integrated DSP processor which has special hardware to 
execute multiply and accumulate functions makes of this core the most avantageous one to 
manage a system of analog-to-digital converters and fetch the digital data that is generated. 
The integrated DSP unit uses a signal processing algorithm to digest the incoming data. The 
results of this signal processing algorithm are used in other engine control algorithms. Using 
the Core_2 to manage the A/D converters and do the initial signal processing of the data 
allows the two other cores to focus on other compute intensive applications instead of 
managing relatively slow peripheral elements.
2.1.4 
Memory hierarchy
The SPC58xHx processing and streaming shells have three levels of memory hierarchy. At 
the top level is a combination of Instruction Cache, Data Cache, Local Instruction RAM and 
Local Data RAM, depending on the specific CPU. The local RAM arrays are embedded into 
the CPU’s pipeline to provide the fastest possible access time. The second level of memory 
is system RAM and flash. These are connected via a 200 MHz, 64-bit wide crossbar. The 
third level of memory system is the I/O subsystem. All the I/O peripherals are connected 
together via a 200 MHz 64-bit wide crossbar switch, while peripherals are connected at 
either 200 MHz or 50 MHz depending on their need. The reduced speed for the peripherals 
helps to reduce power consumption.

Embedded memories
3.1 
Overview
Features include:
•
Onboard SRAM, including system SRAM, local instruction and data memory for each 
processor core
•
Onboard system error correction code (ECC) Flash memory
•
End-to-end ECC (e2eECC) error detection and correction
•
Built-in Flash memory security features including censorship and a programmable 
Hardware Security Module (HSM)
•
Embedded memories in the peripherals(a): 
–
CAN
–
eDMA
–
Ethernet
–
FlexRay
3.2 
SRAM
3.2.1 
System SRAM
SPC58xHx device includes 1088 KB of general-purpose on-chip ECC SRAM, including 
256 KB standby RAM.
•
Refer to  Chapter 34: Platform RAM controller AHB (PRAMC_AHB) for details on 
configuring the SRAM controller.
•
Refer to the Memory Map chapter for the SPC58xHx SRAM map.
3.2.2 
Standby SRAM regulator
A total of 256 KB of the system SRAM on the device can remain powered when the rest of 
the device is powered down. Refer to Chapter 10: Power management for details.
3.2.3 
Processor core local RAM
a.
Refer to the respective module chapter for details.
SPC58xHx devices include local instruction and data RAM (I-MEM and D-MEM) for each 
processor core to provide enhanced performance.
Refer to the Introduction chapter for processor cores local RAM sizes.
The core RAM supports zero wait-state, single-cycle latency on processor local accesses.
Each area of core RAM is accessible by other processor cores and bus mastering 
peripheral devices. Refer to the Memory Map chapter for the SPC58xHx SRAM map.
RM0452 Rev 4
69/3897
RM0452
Embedded memories

3.3 
Embedded Flash memory
Flash memory on SPC58xHx device consists of two Flash memory controllers and a Flash 
memory array module. The Flash controller provides Flash configuration and control 
functions and manages the interface between the Flash memory array and the device 
crossbar switch. Figure 4 shows the memory architecture.
Figure 4. SPC58xHx Flash memory block diagram
The remaining sections give the functional details of the Flash controller and Flash array, 
followed by the memory maps.
3.3.1 
Flash memory controller
The SPC58xHx Flash memory controllers act as an interface between the system bus and 
the Flash memory array.
The Flash memory controller contains a four-entry, two-way set-associative mini-cache that 
delivers Flash read data with a zero-wait state response on lines that reside in the cache. 
Each entry contains one Flash read page, a 256-bit (32-byte) memory value. Read requests 
that miss the cache generate the needed Flash memory array access.
The Flash memory controller contains configuration registers that manage Flash 
functionality such as read buffering in the mini-cache, access control, and read wait state 
management of the Flash memory.
Refer to the Flash memory controller chapter for details.
3.3.2 
Flash memory array
SPC58xHx device includes two Flash memory arrays, one with 4 MB and one with 6 MB, 
referred to as “main space,” plus an independent 16 KB block of one-time-programmable 
(OTP) Flash memory included to support systems that require non-volatile memory for 
security features or system initialization information. The independent 16 KB block is 
referred to as “UTEST space.”

For code Flash sectors, reads of the embedded Flash memory return a 256-bit page of data 
that may be buffered in the mini-cache in the Flash memory controller. Programming of the 
Flash may be done by double word (64-bits), page (256-bits), or quad-page (1024-bits). 
Flash memory is erased on a block by block basis.
3.3.2.1 
Features
•
Flash segmentation
–
16 KB, 32 KB, 64 KB, 128 KB, and 256 KB blocks provided for code or data
–
Four 64 KB blocks provided for EEPROM emulation
–
One 16 KB block and two 64 KB blocks provided for secure code
–
Two 16 KB blocks provided for secure data
–
Support for reading-while-writing when the accesses are to different partitions
•
Flash memory protection: write protection and OTP function available for each block
•
Test and initialization data stored in a non-volatile 16 KB OTP UTEST block
•
ECC with triple bit detection, double and single bit correction
•
Erase suspend, program suspend, and erase-suspended program all supported
3.3.2.2 
Flash organization
The embedded Flash memory consists of six address spaces in four groupings: 
•
16 KB, 32 KB and 64 KB low address spaces
•
16 KB mid address space
•
64 KB high address space
•
256 KB address space
Address space group (low-, mid- or high-address space) determines which registers/fields 
are used to select blocks for modify operations or lock them from modify operations. Each 
address space is independent.
The Flash module is further divided into eight partitions that determine locations for valid 
Read While Write (RWW) operations. While the embedded Flash memory is performing a 
“write” (program or erase) to a given partition, it can simultaneously read from any other 
partition. 
•
For program operations, only the address specified by an interlock write determines the 
partition being written (block locking and block select registers do not determine the 
RWW partitions being written). 
•
For erase operations, only blocks that are selected and unlocked determine the RWW 
partitions being written.
•
For read operation two independent read accesses can be done through both PFlash 
controller to two Read While Read (RWR) partitions.

UTEST memory space
Devices in the SPC58xHx family contain a 16 KB area of one-time-programmable (OTP)

3.3.2.4 
Chip-specific C40FMC Flash register information
Refer to Chapter 36: Embedded Flash Memory for chip-specific layouts of the on-chip Flash 
memory control registers that contain bits used to lock individual Flash blocks from 
accidental erase or select individual Flash blocks for operations.
3.4 
End-to-end Error Correction Code (e2eECC)
To support market requirements related to improved functional and transient fault detection 
capabilities, this family of automotive microcontrollers includes end-to-end ECC (e2eECC) 
support. This e2eECC is structurally different to traditional “ECC at memory” functionality 
because it provides robust error detection capabilities from one endpoint of an information 
transfer to another endpoint, with temporary information storage in one or more intermediate 
components.
Memory protected by ECC/EDC traditionally generates and checks additional error parity 
information local to the memory unit to detect or correct errors that have occurred on data 
stored in the memory, or both. On the other hand, e2eECC generates error protection codes 
at the source of data generation. It sends the encoded data and error protection codes to 
intermediate storage when a memory write is initiated by a bus master and performs a data 
integrity check using the previously stored error protection codes at a data memory when a 
read of stored information is requested by a bus master. The intermediate storage may 
transform the generated error protection codes into another format for storage and then 
regenerate the codes for provision when a request is made to read the stored information or 
it may simply store the original protection codes unaltered, depending on the particular unit.
Additionally, the error protection codes are generated on the basis of more than just the data 
associated with a storage location to protect additional information associated with an 
access. In particular, address information corresponding to the access location of the stored 
information is combined with the stored data at the data source to generate error protection 
codes that cover certain types of addressing errors in the system interconnect or in the 
memory unit. The error protection codes may be checked at the memory unit on a store to 
ensure that no address information or data has been corrupted while the request has 
transitioned through the device from the bus master source. The error protection codes may 
also be checked to ensure that address decoding within the storage memory was performed 
properly (although not all address decoding errors can be detected this way) or it may 
simply store the received data and protection codes at the address it receives.
On a read request from a bus master, the memory unit retrieves the data information and 
error protection codes corresponding to the received address from the storage location or 
locations and supplies the data along with the error protection codes to the requesting 
device. The requesting device uses a locally stored address value corresponding to the 
read request to check the returning data and error protection codes to ensure that no errors 
have occurred in either addressing the memory or in the retrieved data. This ensures that 
the address sent for the request was not corrupted, the addressed location was actually 
accessed (to the extent it is possible to ensure) and the stored data was error free, to the 
extent the ECC coding scheme is able to detect. As a result, the fault coverage provided by 
RM0452 Rev 4
73/3897
RM0452
Embedded memories
74
the end-to-end check is considerably more robust than the previous implementation of 
locally generated and checked/corrected error protection at each memory unit.
A comparison of the traditional and e2eECC approaches is shown in Table 4.
         
The scope of differences in the operations “covered” by the ECC checks is readily apparent 
with the e2eECC concept providing improved fault detection capabilities in two important 
aspects:
•
The entire data transaction; from the initiating bus master, through the entire platform 
crossbar steering mechanism, to the destination slave target is covered during write 
accesses. Likewise, a read is checked from the initiating bus master, through the 
crossbar steering mechanism, through the actual memory read and transmission of the 
data plus checkbits back to the bus master, where the integrity and correctness of the 
entire transaction is checked.
•
The selected ECC provides protection of both the address field as well as the data 
field, again for improved fault coverage.
Additionally, this particular structure also provides a significant implementation 
improvement. The traditional ECC at the memory approach places the checkbit decode and 
error syndrome generation with the error/no_error state, affecting whether the system bus 
transfer must be stalled (to correct a single or double bit error or report a noncorrectable 
event) or is allowed to complete (for error-free transfers) in a critical timing arc which often 
sets the upper limit of the operating frequency of the microcontroller. With the e2eECC 
scheme, the checkbit decode and error syndrome logic is located in the requesting bus 
master where there are generally more degrees of implementation freedom and the

error/no_error state determination is removed from the system bus cycle termination logic; 
producing an improved timing arc and generally higher operating speeds.
Errors that occur within the system interconnect are typically manifested as an incorrect 
address, incorrect write data, or incorrect read data to be presented to the slave or back to 
the master. Errors occurring within the storage typically manifest themselves eventually in 
corrupted read data or checkbits being returned to a requester. While not all possible errors 
can be detected this way, this approach provides a substantial improvement versus 
traditional methods. Additional on-line diagnostics, or additional hardware, or both should be 
able to catch a majority of the errors not covered directly by the e2eECC scheme.
3.5 
Security features
The SPC58xHx architecture implements a security framework that makes it possible to 
protect the micro-controller resources from potential attacks.
Note:
Detailed information on the SPC58xHx security architecture is published in a separate 
document and is available on a limited basis to customers who have a non-disclosure 
agreement (NDA) with STMicroelectronics.

The BGA packages are a superset of the smaller devices. They add only:

Additional GPIO

More analog inputs

New high speed interfaces like SDMMC, Hyperbus, 1Gbps Ethernet RGMII compliant
All but the biggest FPBGA386 packages have been designed to be 100% pin to pin 
compatible with counterpart packages of the SPC58xCx family. Same alternate functions on 
same pads type, same ball/pin built up with same technology M40. These features ease the 
upgrading of existing applications with enriched automotive MCU. Moreover SPC58xHx 
family shows a high level of compatibility with the SPC58xGx MCU family.

Microcontroller Data Sheet.
